mcqs.q: The dental pulp is best defined as:
opts: Richly vascularized and innervated connective tissue of mesodermal origin enclosed by dentin
mcqs.explain: The pulp is a richly vascularized and innervated connective tissue of mesodermal origin, enclosed by dentin and communicating with the PDL.

mcqs.q: Pulpal extensions into the cusps are called:
mcqs.explain: Pulp horns are extensions of the coronal pulp into the cusps; the crown portion is coronal pulp and the root portion is radicular pulp.

mcqs.q: Through the apical foramen pass:
mcqs.explain: The apical foramen is the opening at the root apex through which vascular, lymphatic and nerve elements enter and exit the pulp.

mcqs.q: Accessory canals are clinically significant because they:
opts: Allow spread of infection between pulp and PDL (most numerous in the apical third)
mcqs.explain: Accessory canals run laterally from the radicular pulp to the PDL, are most numerous in the apical third, and are significant in the spread of infection.

mcqs.q: The PRIMARY formative function of the pulp is:
mcqs.explain: The pulp's odontoblasts form primary and secondary dentin, plus tertiary (reparative) dentin in response to stimuli.

mcqs.q: The pulp provides nutrition to the dentin because dentin is:
opts: Not directly supplied by blood vessels
mcqs.explain: Dentin has no blood vessels of its own; the pulp's vessels deliver nutrients and oxygen to it, maintaining tooth vitality.

mcqs.q: The sensory nerves of the pulp are derived mainly from the:
mcqs.explain: The pulp is highly innervated by sensory fibres mainly from the trigeminal nerve, detecting temperature, pressure and pain.

mcqs.q: The regenerative potential of the pulp comes from its:
opts: Mesenchymal stem cells (which can form odontoblast-like cells)
mcqs.explain: The pulp contains mesenchymal stem cells that can differentiate into odontoblast-like cells in response to injury — the basis of regenerative therapies.

mcqs.q: The outermost histological zone of the pulp, at the pulp-dentin border, is the:
mcqs.explain: The odontoblastic zone (palisading odontoblasts) is the outermost zone adjacent to the predentin/pulp-dentin border.

mcqs.q: The cell-free zone of Weil contains the:
mcqs.explain: The cell-free zone of Weil (~40 µm, in coronal pulp) lies just below the odontoblasts and contains the nerve plexus of Raschkow.

mcqs.q: The cell-rich zone of the pulp is:
opts: More prominent in the coronal pulp and rich in fibroblasts
mcqs.explain: The cell-rich zone (more prominent coronally) has a high proportion of fibroblasts plus macrophages, dendritic cells and lymphocytes.

mcqs.q: The MOST numerous cell type in the pulp is the:
mcqs.explain: Fibroblasts are the most numerous pulp cells; they produce type I collagen and ground substance and can also resorb matrix.

mcqs.q: Aged pulp fibroblasts with few organelles and short processes are called:
mcqs.explain: In old pulp, fibroblasts become rounded/spindle-shaped with short processes and few organelles — termed fibrocytes.

mcqs.q: Odontoblasts in the pulp are arranged in a ___ manner:
mcqs.explain: Odontoblasts are arranged in a palisading single row adjacent to the predentin and may crowd to appear pseudostratified.

mcqs.q: The shape of odontoblasts changes from crown to apex as:
mcqs.explain: Odontoblasts are tall columnar in the crown, low columnar mid-root, cuboidal in the root, and flattened at the apex.

mcqs.q: Undifferentiated mesenchymal cells of the pulp are important because they:
opts: Are totipotent and can become odontoblasts, fibroblasts or macrophages
mcqs.explain: Undifferentiated mesenchymal cells (along vessels, in the cell-rich zone) are totipotent and can differentiate as needed; they decrease with age.

mcqs.q: Which is an age (regressive) change of the pulp?
mcqs.explain: Aging brings fibrosis (more collagen), reduced cellularity, vascular changes, pulp stones and diffuse calcification.

mcqs.q: Nodular calcified masses in the coronal or radicular pulp are called:
mcqs.explain: Pulp stones (denticles) are nodular calcified masses found in coronal and radicular pulp; they are usually asymptomatic.

mcqs.q: Diffuse calcification of the pulp (calcific degeneration) appears as:
opts: Irregular calcific deposits following collagen fibres or blood vessels
mcqs.explain: Diffuse calcification (calcific degeneration) consists of irregular calcific deposits, usually following collagenous fibre bundles or blood vessels.

mcqs.q: Pain from the pulp is intense partly because of:
opts: The small volume of the pulp chamber and density of nerve fibres
mcqs.explain: Pulpal pain is intense due to the small, enclosed pulp chamber and the high density of sensory nerve fibres.

mcqs.q: The central region of the pulp contains:
opts: Large nerve trunks and blood vessels
mcqs.explain: The central region of both coronal and radicular pulp contains the large nerve trunks and blood vessels.

mcqs.q: Tertiary (reparative) dentin is formed by the pulp in response to:
mcqs.explain: The pulp forms tertiary/reparative dentin (by odontoblast-like cells) in response to stimuli such as caries, trauma or operative procedures.

mcqs.q: Approximate dimensions of a pulpal odontoblast are:
opts: 5–7 µm in diameter and 25–40 µm in length
mcqs.explain: Pulpal odontoblasts are about 5–7 µm in diameter and 25–40 µm in length, with cell bodies in the pulp and processes in the dentinal tubules.

mcqs.q: Defence cells of the pulp include all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: Pulpal defence cells include macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells, lymphocytes and dendritic cells — not ameloblasts (which form enamel).

saqs.a: A richly vascularized and innervated connective tissue of mesodermal origin, in the centre of the tooth, enclosed by dentin and communicating with the PDL.

saqs.q: Describe the anatomical parts of the pulp.
saqs.a: Coronal pulp (crown, with pulp horns) and radicular pulp (root); the apical foramen transmits vessels/nerves, and accessory canals connect to the PDL.

saqs.q: List the functions of the pulp.
Name the histological zones of the pulp.
saqs.a: Odontoblastic zone, cell-free zone of Weil (with the plexus of Raschkow), cell-rich zone, and central pulp.

saqs.q: What is special about the cell-free zone of Weil?
saqs.a: A ~40 µm zone below the odontoblasts (coronal pulp) that contains the nerve plexus of Raschkow.

saqs.q: Which is the most numerous pulp cell and what does it do?
saqs.a: The fibroblast — it produces type I collagen and ground substance (and can resorb matrix).

saqs.q: List the regressive/age changes of the pulp.
saqs.a: Reduced cellularity, fibrosis (more collagen), vascular changes, pulp stones (denticles), and diffuse calcification.
